ages.note: No age stated; a child can make posters from the fact sheets with a parent.

details: Alley Cat Allies publishes guides and fact sheets for explaining community cats to other people, including 'All About Community Cats' and 'How to Live with Cats in Your Community'.
It treats educating neighbours as a real way to help cats, whether or not you are doing trap-neuter-return yourself.
There is also a workshop guide for teaching a group about community cats and trap-neuter-return.
items.howTo: Read the Educating Others page with a parent, pick a fact sheet, and turn it into a poster or a letter for the street.
items.summary: Use a cat charity's own fact sheets to explain the neighbourhood's outdoor cats to the people who live near them.
items.title: Tell the neighbourhood about community cats

ages.note: Not stated. Fieldwork; ask on the form.

details: Alley Cat Project is 100% volunteer run and foster based, with no physical shelter; its work is trapping, neutering and returning community cats inside Seattle's city limits, north boundary 145th Street.
It supports the people who feed colonies with shelters, feeding stations and food.
No age is stated anywhere; this is fieldwork, so the question to put on the volunteer form is what a parent-and-child pair could do.
items.howTo: Fill in the volunteer form on the homepage and ask what is open to a family.
items.summary: Seattle's all-volunteer, foster-based trap-neuter-return group. No building, no stated age — the volunteer form on its homepage is the way to ask.
items.title: Alley Cat Project: trap-neuter-return in Seattle (age not stated)

ages.note: From age 10 with an adult; alone from 16.

items.commitment: Six months, about eight hours a month.
details: Children under 10 are not eligible; ages 10–15 volunteer with a parent, guardian, grandparent or older sibling who is 18 or over and volunteers too; 16 and over can come on their own.

Under 16 means limited contact with the animals — no dog walking, cat kennel care or cage cleaning. The work is laundry, washing dishes and cat pans, stuffing Kongs, sweeping and mopping, wiping down walls and door handles.
The programme asks for six months and at least eight hours a month, which is about once a week, so it is a standing Saturday rather than a visit.
items.howTo: Apply through the volunteer page once she is 10, together with the adult who will come along — they sign up as a volunteer too.
items.summary: Shelter volunteering that opens at ten with a parent along.
items.title: Auburn Valley Humane Society (from age 10, with an adult)

ages.note: Kindergarten to fifth grade; a parent brings her and signs her in.

items.commitment: Half an hour a session, as often as there is a slot.
details: A year-round reading programme for students in kindergarten to fifth grade: registered readers book 30-minute sessions with the shelter cats and earn a prize for every five they complete.
The cats she reads to are the ones the shelter has cleared for time with children; bring a book or borrow one from the shelter's library.
Sessions run Sunday to Friday, 12pm to 5pm, at the shelter at 4910 A St SE in Auburn. A local news report describes it as free to join.
Applying is a fillable form emailed in, or a paper one at the shelter; places open as there is space, and there is a waitlist when there is not.
This is the one thing at Auburn Valley that is hers alone before ten — their volunteer shifts start at 10 with an adult alongside (listed separately).
items.howTo: Email the Shelter Buddies application from the programme page, then book a 30-minute reading slot once she is registered.
items.location: Auburn Valley Humane Society, 4910 A St SE, Auburn
items.summary: Sign up for a half-hour slot, pick a book, and read it out loud to the cats in the Auburn shelter's cat sanctuary. A prize every five sessions.
items.title: Read to the shelter cats (Shelter Buddies, grades K–5)

ages.note: Not stated.

items.commitment: A volunteer day at a time.
details: The farm welcomes volunteers and schedules ongoing volunteer days throughout the year.
The work is physical — cleaning animal areas — with administrative help and construction for people with that experience. No age is stated.
items.howTo: Sign up for a volunteer day from the volunteer page and ask whether children come.
items.summary: A farm sanctuary in Snohomish County that schedules volunteer days through the year: cleaning animal areas, admin help, construction for those who can.
items.title: Barn Stars farm-animal rescue volunteer days (age not stated)

ages.note: Written for under-18s; no minimum stated.

details: For volunteers under 18, Best Friends lists at-home projects made for the comfort and care of animals at its centers, such as baking dog treats and making cat toys.
Its videos show how to make dog and cat toys from things already around the house: ice-block toys, frozen broth treats, toys from recycled material, and 'Adopt me' bandanas.
Best Friends also has remote roles for adults and a Scout patch program for caring for a kitten in need.
items.howTo: Pick a project from the Best Friends pages, then ask PAWS or RASKC (in this catalog) what they accept before delivering.
items.location: At home; deliver to a local shelter that accepts handmade items
items.summary: A national rescue's list of things kids can make at home for cats and dogs; give them to a local shelter from this catalog.
items.title: At-home projects for shelter animals (Best Friends' ideas for under-18s)

ages.note: No age stated; the volunteer of record is the parent, and writing a pet's bio is something to do together.

details: NOVA (National Operations Volunteers and Ambassadors) lets volunteers lend a virtual hand in real time to Best Friends' centers from anywhere with a secure internet connection; roles include connecting adoptable animals to potential adopters, supporting foster volunteers, record management and pet behavior support.
Remote volunteers also write animal bios, enter data, follow up with adopters, write appreciation notes to members, produce Zoom calls, edit videos and create content.

NOVA volunteers commit to two hours per week; a computer with antivirus protection, an internet connection and a willingness to learn software such as Shelterluv, Trello and Airtable are required; onboarding takes about two weeks.
items.howTo: Apply on the Volunteer From Home page or email nationalvolunteers@bestfriends.org; log the shared hours as entries.
items.summary: Two hours a week from home helping Best Friends' lifesaving centers: pet bios, records, adopter follow-up.
items.title: Best Friends NOVA: remote shelter support (an adult's role, done together)

ages.note: No age stated for the counts; the outings and feeder watches are described as all ages, so start there.

details: Volunteers gather once a month to count birds along a set route in a Seattle park, surveying at points around a loop and entering the results in an online database.
The project monitors bird diversity in city parks and greenspaces across Seattle.
Birds Connect Seattle also runs Neighborhood Bird Outings for whole families, and birdathons and Christmas Bird Count feeder watches that it describes as all ages.
items.howTo: Sign up through the Neighborhood Bird Project page, or join a family Neighborhood Bird Outing first to see how a count works.
items.summary: A monthly bird count in a Seattle park, entered into a database scientists use.
items.title: Neighborhood Bird Project bird counts

ages.note: Under 16 with a parent, on non-animal tasks; 16–17 case by case; 18 for the animals.

details: Under 16, a volunteer may take part only in tasks that do not involve handling animals, and must be accompanied by a parent or guardian. No one under 16 goes into the kennel areas or around the dogs.

The tasks the shelter lists for that: event and fundraising support, organising the retail store and pet pantry, laundry and cleaning, sorting donations, and preparing enrichment items for the animals.
At 16 and 17 the shelter approves volunteers case by case, mainly for school-required hours, with a release form on the first visit; direct work with the animals is 18 and over.
Signing up is the volunteer application (online or in person) and a volunteer orientation booked through SignUpGenius.
items.howTo: Fill in the volunteer application for each of you and book a volunteer orientation from the programme page; she comes to the shifts you take.
items.summary: The Burien shelter takes under-16s on the jobs that keep it running — donation sorting, laundry, making enrichment — with a parent working alongside.
items.title: Burien CARES: sorting, laundry and enrichment with a parent (under 16)

ages.note: A parent is the registered raiser; a child raises alongside.

items.commitment: Daily training and weekly classes, for the puppy's first year and a half.
details: The primary puppy raiser must be 18 or over; minors are allowed to raise with an adult living in the same home, which is the whole family doing it with a parent's name on the form.

Raisers set aside time for daily training and attend puppy classes for the length of the project; where there is no Canine Companions class nearby, an approved public obedience class at your own expense stands in.
A puppy needs 25 to 40 minutes of exercise a day, and cannot go to school with a child in the household.
The Puget Sound chapter is the local community of raisers and graduates; the application takes a few weeks and starts with an application request on the puppy-raising page.
items.howTo: A parent sends the puppy-raising application request from Canine Companions' page, naming her as the minor raising alongside; the Puget Sound field office follows up.
items.location: At home; the Seattle field office and local puppy classes
items.summary: Sixteen months or so with a future service-dog puppy at home. The registered raiser must be an adult, and Canine Companions says minors may raise alongside an adult in the same home.
items.title: Raise a Canine Companions puppy (a parent is the raiser; she helps)

ages.note: Not stated.

details: The coalition does not take in or adopt out cats; its volunteers do independent rescue or work with other rescues, and its focus is TNR training and mentorship.
No age is stated. Contact is CCCofWa@gmail.com.
items.howTo: Email CCCofWa@gmail.com and ask what a family could take on.
items.summary: An all-volunteer coalition with no building that trains and mentors people doing trap-neuter-return, in Snohomish County and beyond.
items.title: Community Cat Coalition: TNR training and mentoring (age not stated)

ages.note: From 18; the keeper path from 21.

details: Applicants must be at least 18 and commit to at least four consecutive hours per scheduled shift.
Roles: docent (education and fundraising), maintenance, fundraising and promotions, landscaping, and keeper aide, which leads toward Volunteer Aide for those with the aptitude — that one is 21.
An online volunteer application; the zoo contacts the people whose applications pass review.
items.howTo: At 18, fill in the online application on the volunteer page.
items.summary: The small zoo on Cougar Mountain takes volunteers from 18 for four-hour shifts: docents, maintenance, landscaping, fundraising, and a keeper-aide path.
items.title: Cougar Mountain Zoo in Issaquah (from 18)

ages.note: A fundraiser is anyone's; the clinic's own volunteers are vets.

items.commitment: A bake sale, a birthday, a lemonade stand.
details: The clinic, renamed Doney Coe in 2018, runs about ten days a month at 1101 Airport Way S and is funded almost entirely by donations.
It says it can no longer accept in-kind donations — public-health directives and storage — so money is what helps; it is on Washington Gives and gifts are tax-deductible.
The volunteers it seeks are veterinary professionals, through volunteer@doneycoe.org.
items.howTo: Run a small fundraiser and give it through the clinic's donate page or Washington Gives.
items.location: Anywhere; the money goes to Airport Way S
items.summary: A Seattle clinic giving free vet care to the pets of people who are homeless or on very low incomes. Since 2021 it cannot take supplies, so a fundraiser is the way a child helps.
items.title: Raise money for the Doney Coe Pet Clinic (money, not supplies)

ages.note: Walks from 6 with an adult; the teaching committee is adults.

details: Eastside Audubon's outings page says its local walks suit families with young birders, and some are geared to families with young children.

The Juanita Bay Park tour is free and open to children 6 and over with an adult; a Confluence Park walk in Issaquah takes children from 10 with a parent; the Bellevue Botanical Garden monthly walk is $5 and needs registration.
Its Youth Education Committee is volunteers who teach children in schools, parks and camps — the role for a parent, with the child along.
items.howTo: Pick a family-suitable walk from the outings page; a parent wanting the teaching side emails youthprograms@eastsideaudubon.org.
items.location: Juanita Bay Park, Kirkland, and other Eastside parks
items.summary: Guided bird walks on the Eastside that take children: Juanita Bay Park from 6 with an adult, free. The volunteer side is adults teaching children.
items.title: Family bird walks with Eastside Audubon (from 6 with an adult)

ages.note: The registered foster is 21+; the child lives with the animal and comes to the meet-and-greet.

items.commitment: A foster at a time, for as long as that animal needs.
details: The registered foster has to be 21 or over, so the parent applies; the rescue asks the entire human household to come to the meet-and-greet — resident dogs too, for a dog foster — which is how a child is part of it from the first day.

Fosters live in the greater Puget Sound area, including Vashon Island, the Olympic Peninsula and within about 30 miles of Seattle, and get the animal to adoption meet-and-greets and vet appointments themselves.
The application asks for a government ID, spay/neuter and vaccination records for pets at home (or a vet's medical waiver), three references, and that you read the Foster Handbook.
items.howTo: A parent applies from the foster page with the ID, pet records and references; then everyone goes to the meet-and-greet.
items.summary: A Seattle rescue that fosters across greater Puget Sound and brings the whole household to the meet-and-greet.
items.title: Foster a dog or cat for Emerald City Pet Rescue (as a family)

ages.note: 16 with a parent; 18 alone.

items.commitment: Three months, at least two shifts a month.
details: Volunteers must be 18 or over, or at least 16 if volunteering alongside a parent or guardian, and pass a background check before a first assignment.
The farm asks for a three-month commitment of at least two shifts a month; the page gives the shift as one hour in one place and two in another, so ask.

Early tasks are stall and enclosure cleaning, cleaning facilities, helping the maintenance team and making content for social media; volunteers are expected to work with all the animals and do all the cleaning that comes with them.
It is a ferry trip: volunteers from off the island provide their own transport to and from the ferry dock, and the sanctuary is not reachable by public transport.
items.howTo: At 16, apply together from the volunteer page; both of you go through the background check and take the shifts as a pair.
items.summary: Emerald City Pet Rescue's sanctuary on Vashon Island, home to ninety-odd horses, donkeys, goats, pigs, cows and llamas. Sixteen with a parent; eighteen alone.
items.title: Ghost Owl Farm sanctuary on Vashon (from 16 with a parent)

ages.note: From 16, per Equine Aid's own posting.

items.commitment: Three to four hours a week.
details: Equine Aid's volunteer posting sets the minimum at 16, asks equine-care volunteers for three to four hours a week, requires an orientation, and says no experience is required.
Applications go to info@equineaid.org.
items.howTo: At 16, email info@equineaid.org for the orientation.
items.summary: Horses, ponies and donkeys in Monroe. Equine Aid's own volunteer posting asks for 16 and over, three to four hours a week, and an orientation; no experience needed.
items.title: Equine Aid horse and donkey sanctuary in Monroe (from 16)

ages.note: No age stated; it is an offsite project for groups and families, with an adult to deliver.

details: Cozy fleece blankets help the shelter's cats and dogs feel warm and safe in their kennels, and are often sent home with the animal when it is adopted.
The shelter's donation page lists fleece blankets and towels among the things it accepts, new, like-new or gently used.
Donations go in the bin on the shelter's front porch, seven days a week between 11am and 5pm — no appointment, no form.
The shelter links a blanket tutorial but cannot provide fleece or other materials.
A group bringing a donation drive can be offered a short tour, arranged beforehand with easvolunteers@everettwa.gov. That is the only part that needs emailing.
items.howTo: Make a batch from the shelter's blanket tutorial and leave them in the donation bin on the front porch any day between 11am and 5pm. Email easvolunteers@everettwa.gov only if you want the tour that goes with a group drop-off.
items.location: At home; deliver to the Everett shelter
items.summary: Fleece blankets that keep shelter cats and dogs warm — and go home with them when they are adopted. Leave them in the donation bin; nothing to arrange.
items.title: Cozy fleece blankets for the Everett shelter

ages.note: From 13, with a parent who trains and works the shift too.

items.commitment: One shift a week, three months at least.
details: Volunteers must be 13 or older, and each programme sets its own age on top of that.
Volunteers aged 13–17 volunteer with a parent or legal guardian, who attends orientation and every training and works the shift with them.
At 16 or 17 some programmes may be done independently if the parent attends training and signs the paperwork; others stay youth-and-adult teams until 18.
The Wing Assistant role is the one the shelter names as good for a junior-and-parent team, from 15.
Most programmes ask for one shift a week for at least three months.
items.howTo: At 13, apply together through the shelter's volunteer application and book orientation for both of you.
items.summary: Shelter shifts alongside a parent once she turns thirteen.
items.title: Everett shelter youth volunteering (13–17, with a parent)

ages.note: No age stated; an adult arranges the drop-off.

details: The shelter always needs food and supplies, and publishes a printable wish list as well as Amazon lists of what is most needed.
Donations can be left in the bin on the front porch, seven days a week between 11am and 5pm.
A group dropping off a donation drive can be given a short tour of the shelter, arranged in advance.
items.howTo: Print the wish list, collect from neighbours or at school, then leave the donations in the porch bin any day between 11am and 5pm — or email easvolunteers@everettwa.gov first if you want the tour.
items.location: Neighborhood or school; deliver to the Everett shelter
items.summary: Collect the food and supplies on the shelter's wish list, with a tour when you deliver.
items.title: Food and supply drive for the Everett shelter

ages.note: From 18, with a background check.

items.commitment: One to four hours a week, May to August.
details: Volunteers must be 18 or over, commit to a one-to-four-hour shift a week from May through August, and pass a Washington State Patrol background check.
Roles include bird care support, maintaining the outdoor aviaries and wash rack, and grounds keeping in the bird garden.

The volunteer page is headed for 2022 and the homepage said the centre was reopening on a limited basis, taking mainly swallows, hummingbirds and birds of prey — ring (253) 350-5792 before relying on any of it.
items.howTo: At 18, apply from the volunteer page; before that, the page is a read.
items.summary: A native-songbird rehabilitator whose volunteer season is May to August, from 18 with a state background check — and which was reopening only on a limited basis when checked.
items.title: Featherhaven songbird rehabilitation in Enumclaw (from 18)

ages.note: Not stated; clinic work.

items.commitment: A weekly or fortnightly shift for three months.
details: Clinic roles include surgery prep, surgery recovery, surgery packs, clinic maintenance and check-in; shifts run two to six hours.
New Lynnwood volunteers commit to a weekly or every-other-week shift for at least three months; experience helps for roles with direct cat contact but is not required.
No age is stated. Applications go through the website or volunteer@feralcatproject.org.
items.howTo: Apply from the volunteer page and ask the minimum age before counting on a role.
items.summary: The free spay/neuter clinic for community cats runs on volunteers: surgery prep, recovery, packing instruments, check-in. Three months of regular shifts; the team trains you.
items.title: Feral Cat Spay/Neuter Project clinic in Lynnwood (age not stated)

ages.note: An adult registers; no age or child rule posted for fostering.

details: Forgotten Dogs Rescue is foster-home based, so fostering is the work; the foster page itself sets out no eligibility.

Its adoption listings say dogs are not placed with families with children under 5 unless a dog's bio says otherwise — an adoption rule, which is the nearest guide to how it thinks about young children.
A virtual Foster Information Session is the stated way to learn the requirements.
items.howTo: A parent signs up for the virtual Foster Information Session from the foster page.
items.summary: A volunteer-and-foster-home rescue for pit-bull-type dogs, in Seattle since 2011. Its foster page gives no criteria; a virtual information session does.
items.title: Foster for Forgotten Dogs Rescue (pit-bull-type dogs)

ages.note: Not stated; high-schoolers are mentioned.

items.commitment: A regular slot for at least two months.
details: Roles: helping at adoption events, walking dogs, transporting dogs, and planning fundraising events.
A downloadable volunteer application, and a regular time of service for at least two months.
The rescue says it has many high-school volunteers and can document hours; parents asking the minimum age in the page's comments got no posted answer.
items.howTo: Download the volunteer application and ask the minimum age when you send it.
items.summary: A Seattle dog rescue that says many high-school students volunteer and that it documents hours; no minimum age is posted.
items.title: Ginger's Pet Rescue: events, walking, transport (age not stated)

ages.note: All ages; a parent sets up the free Cornell Lab account.

items.commitment: Fifteen minutes, one day in February.
details: Four days each February, when people everywhere watch, count and celebrate birds; the count's own pages say it is easy and fun for all ages, whether you count one bird or hundreds.
Fifteen minutes or more, on at least one of the four days, is all it takes.
It is free, and there is no separate registration — you need a free Cornell Lab account through whichever tool you use.
For a beginner with a phone the Merlin Bird ID app is the recommended way in; more practised counters use eBird.
The dates are announced on the count's site each year, so check them rather than assuming.
items.howTo: Check this year's four dates, install Merlin with a parent, and plan the fifteen minutes in the calendar here.
items.summary: Four days every February when the whole world counts birds — fifteen minutes is enough to take part.
items.title: Great Backyard Bird Count

ages.note: Not stated; membership, which is separate, is 18.

details: Kennel turnout is open to volunteers without a greyhound; the Brightwater walks go through a named coordinator; fostering requires that you have or have had a greyhound.
Membership is a separate thing and is 18 and over; volunteers need not be members. No volunteer age is stated.
items.howTo: Ask about turnout from the volunteer opportunities page.
items.summary: Letting the retired racers out at the Woodinville kennel. You do not need a greyhound of your own for turnout; fostering does need greyhound experience.
items.title: Greyhound Pets kennel turnout in Woodinville (age not stated)

ages.note: GDB says raisers can be any age from 9 to 90 and welcomes families; an adult in the house shares the year.

details: Guide Dogs for the Blind says its puppy raisers can be any age, from 9 to 90, and that families are welcome — one of the very few animal programmes that names an age this young.
A puppy arrives at about eight weeks old and goes back to a GDB campus for its formal training between fifteen and seventeen months; raisers teach it good manners and basic obedience in the meantime.
GDB covers veterinary care and provides the equipment and learning materials, including an online Puppy Raising Guidebook.
Washington is one of the states the programme runs in, and raisers belong to a local puppy club.
Giving the puppy back at the end is the hard part, and the reason it matters.
items.howTo: Read the puppy raising pages with a parent, find the nearest puppy club, and apply together — talk first about the day the puppy leaves.
items.location: At home; a puppy club nearby
items.summary: A puppy lives with you for about a year and leaves knowing its manners — and Guide Dogs says raisers can be nine.
items.title: Raise a guide dog puppy

ages.note: No age stated; she needs a camera and an adult's account to upload.

items.commitment: A ferry ride or a whale watch.
details: Happywhale identifies individual whales from photographs and tells you which one you saw.
The matches feed long-term research into where whales travel and how people affect them, shared with whale catalogues including one for the Salish Sea.
The site publishes photography instructions for taking pictures that can actually be matched.
items.howTo: Read the photography instructions first, take fluke and dorsal-fin photos on a ferry or whale watch, then upload them and wait to hear which whale it was.
items.summary: Photograph a whale from a ferry or a whale watch, and find out which individual it was.
items.title: Send whale photos to be identified (Happywhale)

ages.note: Not stated; the 6–12 course is on hold.

details: No experience necessary; the ask is at least fifteen hours of service a year, as a naturalist guide, a docent at the Marine Life Center, or a touch-tank interpreter.
No volunteer age is stated; high-school students earn community service hours here.
A junior naturalist training course for ages 6 to 12 is listed on the programmes page and marked on hold; most programmes are free.
items.howTo: Apply from the volunteer page and ask the minimum age; watch the programmes page for the junior naturalist course to come back.
items.summary: Beach naturalist guides, Marine Life Center docents and touch-tank interpreters, for fifteen hours a year; its junior naturalist course for 6–12s is listed but on hold.
items.title: Harbor WildWatch naturalists in Gig Harbor (age not stated)

ages.note: A drive is anyone's; the drop-off needs a lift.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, one drop-off.
details: Donations can be brought to the Homeward Pet Adoption Center at 13132 NE 177th Place, Woodinville, Tuesday to Sunday 11:30am to 5:30pm; the lobby is closed on Mondays.

Partner shops take donations too — the food bank page lists Mud Bay stores in Bellevue (Overlake) and Bothell, and other pages add Kirkland and shops in Edmonds, Duvall, Kenmore and Mill Creek. The lists differ between pages, so ring (425) 488-4444 before relying on one.
Homeward Pet's preferred contactless route is its Amazon or Chewy wish list, which ships straight to the shelter.
items.howTo: Collect dog and cat food, then take it to the adoption centre in its opening hours or to a Mud Bay that the food bank page lists.
items.location: Neighbourhood or school; drop off in Woodinville or at a partner shop
items.summary: Homeward Pet's pet food bank feeds the pets of people in a hard patch. Collect dog and cat food and drop it at the adoption centre or a partner shop.
items.title: Food drive for Homeward Pet's food bank (Woodinville and the Eastside)

ages.note: The registered foster is an adult; the child helps at home.

items.commitment: Two days to a couple of months per foster.
details: Fostering is described as a great way for families to become involved, especially those with children too young to become volunteers at the shelter.
Foster families provide temporary in-home care, from 2-day kennel breaks to a couple of months of quiet surgery rehab; mostly dogs, from energetic puppies to calm seniors.
The primary foster carer has to be 18 or over, which is the parent; everyone else in the house helps look after the animal.
Fill out the Volunteer Application; you will be invited to the General Orientation.
items.howTo: Submit the Volunteer Application on homewardpet.org and attend the General Orientation.
items.summary: Homeward Pet names fostering as the way in for families whose children are too young to volunteer at the shelter.
items.title: Foster with Homeward Pet (families with young children)

ages.note: Not stated.

details: The help page lists walking and grooming dogs, transporting dogs, building maintenance, and foster homes.
No age is stated; the farm is at 19933 Old Burn Rd, Arlington.
items.howTo: Ring (360) 652-5844 or use the help page and ask what a family can do.
items.summary: A no-kill shelter on a farm that always needs dog walkers, groomers, drivers and foster homes. No age on the page.
items.title: HappyPaws Farm no-kill sanctuary near Arlington (age not stated)

ages.note: An adult registers; Kitsap County homes only.

items.commitment: Two weeks to three months per dog.
details: Fostering covers dogs and puppies, with stays from about two weeks to three months or more.
Foster homes must be in Kitsap County, and fosters return a dog when KARE asks.
items.howTo: A parent applies from the foster page.
items.summary: KARE's fosters take dogs and puppies for two weeks to three months or longer, in homes in Kitsap County, and hand the dog back when KARE asks.
items.title: Foster a dog or puppy for KARE (Kitsap County homes)

ages.note: Most roles 18; under 18 with a parent's permission, no floor given.

details: Most positions require volunteers to be 18; those under 18 need a parent or guardian's permission.
Volunteers must live nearby and have reliable transportation; KARE trains for all positions.
items.howTo: Apply from the volunteer page with a parent's permission and ask which roles take someone her age.
items.summary: A volunteer-powered Kitsap rescue that trains people for every role. Most positions are 18; under 18 needs a parent's permission, and volunteers must live nearby.
items.title: KARE in Kitsap: trained roles, most from 18 (under 18 with a parent's permission)

ages.note: Not stated.

details: Main volunteer opportunities are regular horse care: checking waters, mucking stalls, grooming and, in the rescue's words, loving on the horses.
No age is stated; the rescue names a volunteer coordinator to ask.
items.howTo: Use the volunteering page to reach the volunteer coordinator and ask the minimum age.
items.summary: A horse rescue in the Snoqualmie Valley whose volunteering is the daily care: checking water, mucking stalls, grooming, loving on the horses. No age on the page.
items.title: Kataluna Horse Rescue in Fall City (age not stated)

ages.note: Ages 13–15 per the 2025 volunteer manual, with a parent who also applies.

details: The 2025 volunteer manual defines a youth volunteer as any KHS volunteer aged 13 to 15; a youth volunteer team is a youth and their parent or guardian, or two youths and one adult.
The adult must be an official KHS volunteer, attend every training class alongside her, and stay within sight and within arm's reach for the whole shift.
That adult does not have to be the legal guardian — a grandparent or family friend of 18 or over can do it, with written approval from the parent.
Roles: dog walking, feline socialization, small animal enrichment, laundry and dishes.
items.howTo: Apply together through the volunteer page at 13 — one application each, hers and the adult's.
items.location: Kitsap County, a ferry ride from Seattle
items.summary: Dog walking, cat socialization and small-animal enrichment with a parent alongside.
items.title: Kitsap Humane Society youth volunteers (ages 13–15, with a parent)

ages.note: From 14 with the horses and riders; a few supervised roles under 14 — ask.

items.commitment: A regular shift of an hour and a half to two hours.
details: To work directly with clients and horses a volunteer must be at least 14. The page says limited opportunities exist under 14, provided an adult guardian is present at all times — ask the volunteer office what those are before counting on it.
Shifts run every day of the week and last an hour and a half to two hours.

The first step for an individual volunteer is a one-hour volunteer orientation; the application includes permission for a background check, which applies to adults who volunteer on their own, and the paperwork is renewed yearly to PATH International's standards.
Group volunteering, including the landscaping and gardening days, is 14 and over for everyone in the group.
items.howTo: At 14, book a one-hour volunteer orientation from the volunteer page and apply; before that, email volunteers@littlebit.org to ask what an under-14 can do with you alongside.
items.summary: Horses that help children and adults with disabilities ride. Volunteers lead horses and walk beside riders from 14; a parent-accompanied under-14 route exists but is limited.
items.title: Little Bit Therapeutic Riding Center (from 14; a few roles under 14 with an adult)

ages.note: The registered foster is an adult over 18; the child helps at home.

details: Foster homes must be over 18, so a parent is the registered foster and the whole family helps at home.
MEOW says it has only limited opportunities for under-18s and cannot offer teens work that meets school service-hour requirements — fostering is what it suggests for families.
It is currently taking applications for fosters as well as kennel attendants and shelter assistants.
items.howTo: Email volunteer@meowcatrescue.org to reach the Volunteer Programs Manager and ask to foster as a family.
items.summary: A Kirkland cat rescue that points families who want to help together towards fostering.
items.title: Foster cats with MEOW Cat Rescue (as a family)

ages.note: A parent is the registered foster; children in the home are not addressed on the page — ask.

items.commitment: Two weeks at least, an hour twice a day.
details: Three kinds of stay: a two-week quarantine for each new arrival before it joins the café, medical stays, and behavioural stays for cats that find the busy lounge too much.
Food, litter and the basics are provided by the Foundation. A foster home either has no other pets or can keep the foster cat separate from them.

The ask is at least two weeks, about an hour twice a day on care and company, a car to collect and return the cat, and a home within 45 minutes of the café on N 45th St. The Foundation wants families who will foster again, and says it is not the place for fostering in order to adopt.
The foster page does not say whether children in the home are a problem; the adoption FAQ welcomes families with children, cat by cat. Ask on the application.
items.howTo: A parent fills in the foster application on the café's site, saying there is a child at home and that you would foster more than once.
items.summary: Meowtropolitan Foundation is the rescue behind Seattle's cat café. Its fosters take a cat for the two-week quarantine before the lounge, or for a medical or behavioural stay.
items.title: Foster a cat for the Wallingford cat café's rescue (as a family)

ages.note: From 16.

details: Volunteers must be at least 16 and physically able to lift at least 40 pounds; comfort with customers and some knowledge of animals are preferred.
Questions go to 253-299-PETS ext 2 or pets@sumnerwa.gov. The shelter is at 1200 39th Ave SE, Puyallup, run by the City of Sumner.
items.howTo: At 16, apply from the volunteering page.
items.summary: The shelter serving Sumner, Puyallup, Bonney Lake and Edgewood takes volunteers from 16 who can lift forty pounds.
items.title: Metro Animal Services shelter in Puyallup (from 16)

ages.note: No minimum for the children in a cat foster home (dogs need them over 5); the adult is the registered foster.

details: On-site volunteering at Motley Zoo's boarding and training facility is 18+, so fostering at home is how a family takes part.

The age rule is about the animal, not the volunteer: dogs go only to homes where the children are over 5, while cats, kittens and other small animals can go to families with children under 5, at Motley Zoo's discretion.
Fostering cats does not need much space: a half-bath or laundry room is plenty for a litter box, bowls and a soft place to nap, and Motley Zoo can provide the supplies, including food.
items.howTo: Email cats@motleyzoo.org about fostering kittens as a family, or info@motleyzoo.org for how to get involved.
items.summary: A Redmond rescue whose cat fostering is open to households with children too young for anywhere else.
items.title: Foster kittens with Motley Zoo (young children welcome)

ages.note: An adult applies; nothing said about children at home.

details: NEKO looks for fosters of every level of cat experience with the space and time to socialise cats, transport, and a home near its Seattle location; it supplies the cats, the supplies and support.
Applying is a resume sent to info@nekocatcafe.com or brought in, naming the location. No age is stated; the café itself is open to all ages, which is a visitor rule.
items.howTo: A parent emails a short resume to info@nekocatcafe.com for the Seattle location, saying there is a child at home.
items.location: At home; near the Seattle café
items.summary: NEKO has no in-house volunteer roles but wants home fosters near its Seattle café, with cats, supplies and support provided. It is a business, not a charity.
items.title: Foster for NEKO Cat Café (a café that fosters for rescues)

ages.note: 12–18 with a parent or guardian; under 12 not allowed.

items.commitment: Two hours a week for six months.
details: Volunteers between twelve and eighteen must be accompanied by a parent or guardian; for liability reasons the farm cannot take anyone under twelve.
Regular volunteers commit to a two-hour shift once a week for at least six months, after an initial orientation; the page listed weekday openings, and says to email for what is open now.
It is a working farm: feeding, mucking out and the care of animals that arrived in poor shape.
items.howTo: At 12, email volunteer@newmoonfarm.org together to ask for the orientation and a weekly slot you can both keep.
items.summary: An Arlington sanctuary for rescued goats. Volunteers from 12 come with a parent; the ask is a two-hour shift a week for six months.
items.title: New Moon Farm goat sanctuary (from 12, with a parent)

ages.note: An adult is the registered foster — Old Dog Haven's volunteers are all 18+; a gentle old dog is easy company for a child.

details: Old Dog Haven is a network of private homes across western Washington, Spokane and Portland, taking homeless dogs aged eight and over and prioritising the oldest and sickest.
Its greatest need is Final Refuge homes, where a dog with age- and health-related needs stays for as long as it has a good quality of life.
Old Dog Haven pays all medical costs including prescription food; the family pays the everyday costs of having a dog.
Old Dog Haven asks that every volunteer be 18 or over, so the adult in the house is the registered one and the child lives with the dog rather than signing up for anything.
items.howTo: Read the fostering page with a parent, then fill in the volunteer package and email it to office@olddoghaven.org.
items.summary: A network of homes across western Washington caring for dogs aged eight and over.
items.title: Foster an old dog (Old Dog Haven)

ages.note: No age stated; a child watches and describes, a parent sends the report.

details: Orca Network's Whale Sighting and Education Project collects sightings of orcas and every other cetacean of the Salish Sea.
A report says when you saw them, the species, how many, where, which way they were heading and what they were doing, and whether you have photos — photos can be emailed to sightings@orcanetwork.org.
The network publishes a map of shoreline viewpoints from Deception Pass to Olympia, so a report can start with choosing where to stand.
It also points at Orcasound's hydrophones for listening when there is nothing to see.
items.howTo: Pick a viewpoint from the map, take binoculars, and send what she sees through the sightings report page — log the watching as an entry either way.
items.summary: Watch the water from a shoreline viewpoint, and tell the network what went past.
items.title: Report a whale sighting to Orca Network

ages.note: No age stated; listening needs nothing but headphones, and a parent can set it up.

details: Orcasound streams live hydrophones — underwater microphones — from locations around Puget Sound; you open live.orcasound.net and pick one to listen to.

Listeners tell the network when they hear orcas or any sound that might matter, which helps researchers learn when and where the endangered Southern Residents travel, how they communicate and forage, and what noise may be holding back their recovery.
Anyone is welcome to join the network for free as a citizen scientist.
items.howTo: Open live.orcasound.net, choose a hydrophone and listen; report what she hears, and log the listening time as an entry.
items.summary: Headphones, a live hydrophone in Puget Sound, and a button to press when she hears a whale.
items.title: Listen for orcas on live underwater microphones

ages.note: Booked by a teacher for a fourth-grade class, not by a family.

details: PAWS's school programmes include the signature six-week Kids Who Care programme for fourth-grade classrooms, and individual class projects.

PAWS education runs September through May and reaches more than 3,000 youth and adults a year with a six-lesson programme for elementary schools, live workshops at PAWS, badge programmes and projects helping animals.
items.howTo: Send the School Year Programs page to her teacher, or email education@paws.org and ask them to approach the school.
items.summary: PAWS's signature six-week programme, taught in the classroom — one for her teacher.
items.title: Kids Who Care, for fourth-grade classrooms

ages.note: No age limit stated; written for kids.

details: PAWS's Youth Projects page is the list: snuffle mats, cardboard cat scratchers, dog toys from old t-shirts or jeans, cat toys from fabric, feathers and string, and cat beds sewn from used sweaters.
The scratchers come with a size — 3.5" x 8", with a twist tie so one hangs on a kennel door.
At PAWS you have to be 18 or over to work with or around animals, so things made at home are how someone younger helps the animals directly.

Handmade things are not on the printed wish list, and PAWS asks that anything not on it be checked with them first, and that donations be dropped off in business hours arranged by phone on 425.787.2500. It has had a lot of bedding donated lately, so that call is what decides between beds and scratchers.
PAWS also suggests being kind to wildlife at home: fresh water and bird feeders, and picking up litter that can harm wild animals.
items.howTo: Ring PAWS on 425.787.2500 to ask which projects they are short of and when to bring them, then make a batch from the Youth Projects page.
items.location: At home; deliver to PAWS in Lynnwood
items.summary: PAWS keeps its own list of things to make at home for the shelter's cats and dogs. Ring first to hear what they are short of, then make a batch.
items.title: Make cat toys, scratchers and beds for PAWS

ages.note: Open to 9–11 year olds; an adult stays for the workshop.

details: In Our Wild World, participants learn about the habitats local wildlife call home and how to protect them, and receive a PAWS fun patch; it fulfils all the requirements for the Girl Scout Junior Animal Habitats badge.
Individual Girl Scouts, and up to four girls from the same troop, are welcome — it does not have to be booked as a whole troop.
In person at PAWS and approximately 90 minutes; not a drop-off programme, so a parent, guardian or troop leader stays. Offered in partnership with Girl Scouts of Western Washington.
PAWS runs the same workshops at other Scout levels, so there is one for later: Caring Creatures (Daisy), PAWS for Cats and Dogs (Brownie Pets badge) and Heroic Animal Helpers (Cadette, ages 11–13).
items.howTo: Watch PAWS's Scout Programs page for the next Our Wild World date and book her in individually; email education@paws.org to ask when the next one is.
items.summary: A ninety-minute workshop at PAWS on the habitats local wildlife live in — and she is exactly the right age.
items.title: Our Wild World: Junior Animal Habitats badge at PAWS

ages.note: From 16 with a parent's approval; 18 for the adult role.

details: Cat City Support Volunteer – Teen is for 16 and over: reliable transport to Cat City, parent or guardian approval, orientation, a CAS information session and skills training, and a background check. The adult Cat City Assistant role is 18.
Both listings said applications were closed and shifts filled; PAWS says Cat City has very limited open shifts for adults and teens at this time.
Cat City is at 5200 Roosevelt Way NE, Suite B, in the University District.
items.howTo: At 16, watch the teen listing for shifts to reopen, then apply with a parent's approval.
items.summary: PAWS's Seattle cat adoption centre has a teen support role from 16: enrichment and cleaning, with a parent's approval, training and a background check. Shifts were all filled when checked.
items.title: PAWS Cat City in the U District, teen role (from 16)

ages.note: No age limit stated; collecting and delivering needs an adult.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, then one delivery or shipment.
details: PAWS publishes a downloadable list of what it needs now, and Amazon and Chewy wish lists whose items ship straight to the shelter — nothing to carry and nothing to arrange.
It cannot take food or treats that have been opened or are past their date.
PAWS's kids and teens page says children often ask for donations to help animals instead of birthday presents, and can run a FUNdraiser, a gift drive, or collect supplies — or all three.
Anything not on the list, and any drop-off in person, goes through a call to 425.787.2500 first.
items.howTo: Open the wish list, either have the items shipped to PAWS from the Amazon list or collect them from neighbours and school, and ring 425.787.2500 before bringing anything in person.
items.location: Neighborhood or school; ship or deliver to PAWS
items.summary: Collect supplies from PAWS's wish list, or ask for donations instead of birthday presents.
items.title: Wish-list drive or birthday donations for PAWS

ages.note: From 16.

items.commitment: One shift a week, an hour and a half to two hours.
details: Volunteers must be 16 or over and commit to a shift of an hour and a half to two hours each week.
Most roles mean standing for the shift and climbing a couple of flights of stairs.
It is a small place — visits by appointment, and the shelter is open to the public only on some weekday afternoons — so ring before going.
items.howTo: At 16, ring (360) 373-7043 or apply from the volunteer page; the ferry to Bremerton is part of the trip.
items.summary: A volunteer-run, cat-only, no-kill shelter in Bremerton. Everyone there is a volunteer; the minimum age is 16 and the ask is one shift a week.
items.title: PAWS of Bremerton cat shelter (from 16)

ages.note: From age 12 alongside a legal guardian.

details: Volunteer opportunities are available for youths 12 and older; volunteers 12–15 must volunteer alongside a legal guardian; 16 and 17 may volunteer with guardian consent and a background check.
Signing up is an online application with a background check — for a twelve-year-old that falls on the guardian who comes along.
Compassion Days group volunteer events are for groups 18 and older, typically 10:00 a.m.–2:30 p.m.
items.howTo: Email volunteer@pasadosafehaven.org or call (360) 793-9393 when she is 12.
items.summary: A sanctuary in Sultan for rescued farm animals, dogs and cats.
items.title: Pasado's Safe Haven farm sanctuary (from age 12, with a guardian until 16)

ages.note: From 10, with an adult present at every visit until 16; needs a pet of your own.

items.commitment: A course and an evaluation, then visits you choose.
details: Handlers can be as young as 10. Under 16, a parent, guardian or another approved adult is present on every visit; under 18, a signed permission form from the parent. The criminal background check is for handlers 18 and over only.

The animal has to be at least a year old at evaluation (six months for rabbits, guinea pigs and rats) and have lived in your home for at least six months, and a vet completes Pet Partners' own health screening form.
Becoming a team is a handler course ($80 online), then a team evaluation with a local evaluator (typically $15–30), then registration ($95 for a new team, $70 to renew).
Facilities set their own limits on top of that, and some have age limits of their own.
items.howTo: At 10, with a pet that has lived with you six months, take the handler course together, book a team evaluation, and register.
items.location: Wherever the visit is — a library, a hospital, a care home
items.summary: Pet Partners registers handlers from age ten — with a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig of your own — to visit hospitals, libraries and care homes.
items.title: Visit with your own pet as a therapy animal team (from age 10)

ages.note: Not stated.

details: The sanctuary is open May 1 to November 1 and closed the rest of the year; when open, every visit is by appointment.
House rules: no smoking, weapons, drugs or alcohol, and no personal pets on the grounds; the animals' needs come first.
Volunteers mainly scoop manure, with occasional work parties; no age is stated. Contact pigspeace@gmail.com; two different phone numbers are published, so email first.
items.howTo: Email pigspeace@gmail.com to ask about a visit first, and whether a family can help on a work party.
items.summary: A sanctuary for cast-off pigs. Open to visitors May to November by appointment; volunteering is mostly manure scooping and work parties, no age stated.
items.title: Pigs Peace Sanctuary in Stanwood (visits by appointment; volunteering is manure)

ages.note: Youth release form on trips; no age given.

details: The upcoming-trips page carries both an adult and a youth release form, so young birders join scheduled outings with an adult.
Puget Sound Bird Fest, in Edmonds each June, includes a Kids' Corner.
An Audubon for Kids page lists activities to do at home or in a yard or park.
items.howTo: Choose a trip from the upcoming-trips page and send the youth release form with hers.
items.location: Snohomish County parks; Edmonds for the Bird Fest
items.summary: Snohomish County's Audubon chapter runs public field trips with a youth release form, and a Puget Sound Bird Fest each June with a Kids' Corner.
items.title: Pilchuck Audubon field trips and the June Bird Fest (with an adult)

ages.note: From 14 (16 for beach walks), with an adult until 18.

items.commitment: A training, then surveys she schedules herself across a season.
details: Spot the Swallows is open from 14: after a training session volunteers schedule their own surveys of nest-box sites at Point Defiance Park, Titlow Beach Park or Chinese Reconciliation Park through spring and summer, and the data goes to the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife.

Larval Crab Monitoring is also from 14: checking a light trap at the Point Defiance Boathouse for Dungeness crab larvae with the Pacific Northwest Crab Research Group, after learning crab life history and plankton identification.
Beach Walk Naturalist is from 16 — talking to beach-goers at low tide.
Under 18 needs an adult along for all three. Almost all of it happens away from the zoo, and it is seasonal: spring and summer.
items.howTo: Watch the community science page for a project with applications open — they are seasonal — and apply together.
items.location: Point Defiance Park, Titlow Beach and the Point Defiance Boathouse, Tacoma
items.summary: The zoo's community science runs away from the zoo, on Tacoma's parks and beaches: swallow nest boxes, a crab light trap at the boathouse, low-tide beach walks.
items.title: Count swallows and crab larvae with the zoo (from 14, with an adult)

ages.note: Ages 14–18, in grades 9–12.

items.commitment: Spring training, then a six-hour shift a week all summer.
details: For 14- to 18-year-olds in grades 9 to 12; graduating seniors can still apply.
The zoo is clear that Zoo Guides do not help with animal care — the role is visitor-facing.

Applications open in December. Applicants do an informal group interview and orientation, then training starts in late March: seven to nine required sessions through June, followed by one six-hour shift a week for nine or ten weeks of the summer season.
Apply at pdza.org/volunteer when the window is open; outside it there is a waitlist form, which the zoo says is not an application.
items.howTo: Apply in December of 8th or 9th grade for the summer that follows; the volunteer page carries the form while it is open.
items.summary: A summer as a youth ambassador at the Tacoma zoo and aquarium: trained in the spring, one six-hour shift a week through the summer, talking to visitors.
items.title: Point Defiance Zoo Guides (ages 14–18)

ages.note: Under 16 with an adult; no floor stated.

details: All are welcome to volunteer; minors under 16 must be accompanied by an adult.
The page warns that the work on the farm can be quite repetitive, physically demanding and messy.
Adopting a horse is 21 and over, which is a different rule from volunteering.
items.howTo: Sign up from the volunteer page together and ask which days the farm takes helpers.
items.location: Olalla, across the water from Seattle
items.summary: A Kitsap-side rescue for horses out of the slaughter pipeline whose volunteer page says all are welcome and under-16s come with an adult. Repetitive, physical, messy — their words.
items.title: Pony Up horse rescue in Olalla (under 16 with an adult)

ages.note: All skill levels and backgrounds, children and families included; a parent signs up and pays the fee.

items.commitment: Two days at a time, weekly at most, November to April.
details: A November-to-April survey of the birds visiting yards and other places across North America, run by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Birds Canada.
It names children and families among the people who do it — some families count together as a way of learning the birds in their own garden.

Choose a patch you can watch easily; you do not need to put out feeders. Count on two days in a row, as often as once a week, leaving at least five days between counts, and record the most of each species you can see at one moment.
Counts are submitted on the website or the FeederWatch app.

There is a participation fee — $18 in the US, $15 for Cornell Lab members — which pays for the database and the project materials. A first season is free with the code FIRSTPFW at checkout, and an educational group leader can use PFWEDU for $5 off.
items.howTo: Sign up with a parent before November (the code FIRSTPFW makes a first season free), choose the patch to watch, and put the count days in the calendar here.
items.summary: Pick a spot you can see from a window and count who visits, two days at a time, all winter.
items.title: Project FeederWatch: count the birds in your own yard

ages.note: From 18.

details: At this time the rescue does not allow children under 18 to volunteer.
A visit is a three-hour shift.
items.howTo: At 18, use the get-involved page.
items.summary: A goat rescue in Maple Valley whose shifts are three hours and whose volunteers are adults — it says it does not allow anyone under 18.
items.title: Puget Sound Goat Rescue (from 18)

ages.note: An adult is the trained foster; twice-daily feeding and litter is real work a child can share.

items.commitment: A night to ten weeks, and you choose each time.
details: Purrfect Pals needs foster homes for kittens too young to be adopted, and for a mother cat with her kittens — for a single night, or for several weeks.
Fosters are trained at Arlington and then put on call, and can always say no to a litter when the timing is wrong.

What a home needs: a safe room shut away from your own pets (a bedroom, bathroom or laundry room is enough), your own pets up to date on vaccines, fresh food, water and clean litter twice a day, and the foster cats kept indoors.
A mother cat with newborns needs nine or ten weeks; an adult cat who is low needs two to four.
items.howTo: Fill in the foster application with a parent, then go to a training session at Arlington together.
items.location: At home; training and pick-up in Arlington
items.summary: A cat sanctuary's foster list: kittens too young to be adopted, sometimes for a single night.
items.title: Foster kittens for Purrfect Pals

ages.note: From age 13; under 16 with a parent or guardian.

details: At the main sanctuary in Arlington, volunteers must be 13 or older, and anyone under 16 must be with a parent or guardian.
Volunteers organize fundraising events, sew cat blankets, brush cats, pick up donations, maintain sanctuary grounds, take photos of cats, and more.
Ongoing project needs at the sanctuary include gardening and landscaping, maintenance, painting, cleaning and construction.
items.howTo: Email volunteers@purrfectpals.org from the volunteer page when she turns 13.
items.summary: The region's first no-kill cat shelter, on five acres in Arlington.
items.title: Purrfect Pals cat sanctuary (from age 13, with a parent until 16)

ages.note: From 16, no exceptions.

details: Minimum age 16, no exceptions, because of the shelter's insurance; a three-month commitment and a liability waiver; applications are reviewed and approved before anyone starts.
Its community outreach programme welcomes groups of all ages to visit and learn about rabbit care — a visit, not a shift.
items.howTo: At 16, apply from the volunteer page; before that, a group visit is the way in.
items.summary: A rabbit shelter whose insurance sets the volunteer age at 16 with no exceptions; groups of any age can visit to learn rabbit care.
items.title: Rabbit Haven in Gig Harbor (from 16)

ages.note: No age limit — anyone can make and donate. Sharp scissors and the drive to Kent need an adult.

details: This one is a donation, not a volunteer role: RASKC's wish list asks for "yards of fleece for making cat blankets (or make your own to donate)". No application, no agreement form, no orientation — make them and bring them.

No sewing needed: cut fleece 25" x 21" for a large blanket or 13" x 21" for a small one, then cut the edges into fringe and tie it. RASKC's instruction sheet says the fringe has to be tied very tightly, because loose fringe is dangerous for a cat.
If you do sew, the sizes are 22" x 18" or 10" x 18". Fleece only, either way.
Take them to the Pet Adoption Center, 21615 64th Ave S in Kent, which is open to the public weekdays 12–6pm and weekends 12–5pm except major holidays.

Service hours are the one part that needs arranging first. RASKC credits an hour per blanket, but only in the months it is taking them, and asks that blanket-making be scheduled before you start — email RASKC.Volunteers@kingcounty.gov. Donating without counting hours needs none of that.
RASKC's volunteer page lists blankets under group volunteering too, alongside running a small fundraiser, putting up posters in the community, and making videos.
items.howTo: Cut and tie a batch to the sizes on RASKC's instruction sheet, then take them to the Kent Pet Adoption Center any afternoon it is open. Email RASKC.Volunteers@kingcounty.gov first only if you want the hours credited as community service.
items.location: At home; drop off at the Kent shelter
items.summary: Make fleece blankets at home and drop them off. RASKC's wish list asks for them, so there is nothing to apply for — every cat gets one in its condo and takes it home when it is adopted.
items.title: Cat cozy blankets for the Kent shelter

ages.note: The registered foster is 16+, in practice a parent; children help care for the cat at home.

details: The foster applicant must be at least 16 and an adult in the household signs the liability waiver, so a parent registers and the family fosters together.
To foster rather than take shifts, RASKC asks for one online application for the household instead of one each — everyone at home is still welcome to help with the animal.
Getting started is that application plus the Fostering 101 training video and a quiz.
After training you join waitlists for the kinds of animal you would like to foster; when one is ready an email comes and it needs answering quickly.

RASKC's volunteer page also says children can take part in caring for animals through fostering, with an adult in the household as the official volunteer — which is how a nine-year-old helps here, since shelter shifts start at nine only with a parent alongside.
items.howTo: A parent fills in one online volunteer application for the household and signs the agreement form, you watch Fostering 101 together and take the quiz, then pick the cat waitlists.
items.summary: Train once, join the waitlist for the animals you want, then say yes when an email comes.
items.title: Foster a cat for the Kent shelter (RASKC)

ages.note: From age 9 with a parent or guardian; 16–17 with consent.

items.commitment: Scheduled shifts, typically an hour or two.
details: RASKC offers volunteer opportunities for ages 16 and 17 with guardian consent, and ages 9–15 with an accompanying guardian.
The Shelter Helper role is available for ages 9+; youth 9–15 must be accompanied by their parent or legal guardian, who becomes a volunteer too and supervises.
Listed Shelter Helper shifts involve laundry, washing and sanitising water bowls and litter boxes, preparing cat-food trays and taking the rubbish out, at the Kent Pet Adoption Center.

Signing up is three things: the online volunteer application, which a parent/youth team fills in separately for each person who wants a shift; a volunteer agreement form, which only an adult can sign; and a new-volunteer orientation — in person in Kent about twice a month, a few times a year on the Eastside, or online for anyone who cannot get to one.
RASKC then gets in touch about which open roles match, and training is reading material plus apprenticeship shifts alongside a mentor volunteer.
Shelter Helper asks for six months, or six shifts plus two training shifts over a summer.
Questions go to RASKC.Volunteers@kingcounty.gov.
items.howTo: Each of you fills in the online volunteer application, a parent signs the volunteer agreement form, then you both go to a new-volunteer orientation and RASKC matches you to Shelter Helper shifts.
items.location: Kent Pet Adoption Center, 21615 64th Ave S, Kent
items.summary: Real shelter chores for kids as young as nine, alongside a parent or guardian.
items.title: Shelter Helper at the Kent shelter (from age 9 with a parent)

ages.note: 8–15 with a parent volunteering alongside; 16 for barn-chore shifts on your own.

details: SAFE's minor-volunteer agreement says a child aged 8 to 15 can volunteer only when a parent or legal guardian who is also volunteering is present for the whole visit; the regular chore shifts are 16 and over.

The rules for a child are precise: stay within about ten feet of the parent at all times, never enter a paddock or pasture with horses in it, and never enter a stall with a horse inside. Breaking them ends the child's volunteering.

The team SAFE's own postings describe as a fit for children and teens is the Saturday grounds crew, 10am to 1pm — gardening and landscaping around the barn, which is how an eight-year-old helps a horse rescue without being in with the horses.
The adult goes through the volunteer profile and a short orientation first; the postings say the orientation is an introduction to SAFE and the place to ask questions.
items.howTo: The parent fills in SAFE's volunteer profile and books the orientation from the volunteer page, signs the minor-volunteer agreement for her, and you join the Saturday grounds team together.
items.summary: A horse rescue near Woodinville with a written rule for children: 8 to 15 may volunteer when a parent is volunteering beside them for the whole visit.
items.title: Saturday grounds team at SAFE horse rescue (from 8, with a parent)

ages.note: 12–14 with an adult throughout; 14–16 with experience; 16 alone.

details: Individual volunteers must be at least 16 and able to work independently; 14- to 16-year-olds are considered only with substantial prior experience; children of 12 to 14 can volunteer if an adult stays with them at all times.
Older coverage says the sanctuary also looked for volunteers from 13 to help run its summer camps — ask whether that still holds.
The sanctuary is open to visitors, which is how a younger child sees it first.
items.howTo: At 12, apply from the individual-volunteer page naming the adult who will stay with her.
items.summary: A farm-animal sanctuary on the Eastside with a three-step age rule on its own page: 12 to 14 with an adult who stays the whole time, 14 to 16 only with real experience, 16 on your own.
items.title: Sammamish Animal Sanctuary (from 12 with an adult; 16 alone)

ages.note: No age stated for a drive; an adult arranges the delivery.

details: Sarvey treats around 3,000 wild patients a year and depends on donations; the average cost of a patient is about $200.
It publishes an everyday donation wish list, and also takes contributions through its Amazon wish list.
Hands-on volunteering there is physically demanding outdoor work in all weather, so a drive is the way a younger child helps.
items.howTo: Print the everyday wish list, collect the items, then ring (360) 435-4817 to arrange dropping them off.
items.location: Neighborhood or school; deliver to Arlington
items.summary: Collect what a wildlife hospital needs for the three thousand wild animals it treats a year.
items.title: Wish-list drive for Sarvey Wildlife Care Center

ages.note: An adult registers; children in the home must be 6 or over.

items.commitment: A few weeks or more per dog.
details: The ask is a home for a few weeks or more; the rescue takes care of vet bills and you provide food and bedding.
Foster dogs cannot be placed in homes with children under 6.
Applying is the foster application, the foster guide, and the foster waiver; volunteer questions go to lily@savinggreatanimals.org. No volunteer age is stated — the adult registers.
items.howTo: A parent fills in the foster application, reads the guide and signs the waiver.
items.summary: A Seattle dog rescue that covers vet bills while you give a dog a home for a few weeks or more. Foster dogs do not go to homes with children under 6.
items.title: Foster a dog for Saving Great Animals (homes with children 6 and over)

ages.note: No age on the current page; Seal Sitters has said children are welcome with a parent. Confirm when you sign up.

items.commitment: A two-hour training, then beach shifts when a pup comes ashore.
details: Seal Sitters is West Seattle's all-volunteer marine mammal stranding network. Everyone who volunteers first attends a training session covering seal biology, beach protection protocols and talking to the public; trainings are typically held each spring before the busy season.

The current volunteer page does not state a minimum age. Seal Sitters' own earlier posts say that, unlike most stranding networks, it encourages children to take part, supervised at all times by a parent or guardian — and that a child must be able to sit through the roughly two-hour training. Ask when you join the list.
Trained volunteers cover the beaches from Brace Point through the Duwamish River, including Harbor Island; there are also roles off the beach, as hotline operator, first responder or scheduler.
To be told about the next training, email from the volunteer page or fill in the Volunteer Interest form, which puts you on the waiting list.
items.howTo: Fill in the Volunteer Interest form to join the waiting list for the spring training, and ask whether she can train alongside you.
items.location: West Seattle beaches, Brace Point to the Duwamish
items.summary: When a harbor seal pup hauls out to rest on a West Seattle beach, Seal Sitters put a volunteer on the sand to keep people and dogs back and explain why. All ages have done it, with a parent.
items.title: Seal Sitters: keep watch over a seal pup on a West Seattle beach

ages.note: The registered foster is an adult; the child helps at home.

details: To volunteer at the Seattle Animal Shelter you must be 18 or older; family participation is allowed and encouraged through fostering.

The shelter says fostering can build a foundation of philanthropy in your children, to select a cat that is age-appropriate for them, and to give children guidance, instructions and rules about caring for an orphaned cat.
A Kitten Care class is offered when more kitten fosters are needed.
items.howTo: Complete the online volunteer profile and select Foster Care Volunteer–Cats.
items.location: At home; the shelter is at 2061 15th Ave W, Seattle
items.summary: The city shelter calls fostering a wonderful family experience; shelter volunteering itself starts at 18.
items.title: Foster Cat Program (Seattle Animal Shelter)

ages.note: A drive is anyone's; the drop-off needs a lift.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, one drop-off.
details: The donate page links the shelter's Amazon wish list and a printable version, and says donated items can be dropped off during business hours — it does not list the hours, so ring 206-386-7387 first.
The shelter also runs a pet food bank for people who cannot afford to feed their animals, so food is never wasted on it.
Items bought from the wish list online ship straight to the shelter, which is the route that needs no drop-off at all.
items.howTo: Print the wish list, collect, ring the shelter for its drop-off hours, and take it in — or have people buy from the online list and skip the trip.
items.location: Neighbourhood or school; drop off at 2061 15th Ave W
items.summary: The city shelter on 15th Ave W keeps a wish list and takes items in business hours. The nearest shelter to most of Seattle to run a drive for.
items.title: Wish-list drive for the Seattle Animal Shelter

ages.note: Grades 9–12.

details: Open to students in grades 9–12 — high school, Running Start, GED or homeschool at the time of applying — who volunteer on marine conservation and advocacy.
You cannot apply cold: everyone attends one of the online information sessions first, and the application comes after that.
The Aquarium then interviews from the applicant pool and chooses on the interview and the application together.
The school-year round runs to a calendar: the interest form opens in August, the Zoom information sessions are in September, applications go in during October, and decisions follow.
items.howTo: Fill in the interest form when it opens in August — that is the step with a deadline; the information session in September and the October application follow from it.
items.summary: High-schoolers volunteer for marine conservation and advocacy at the Aquarium.
items.title: Youth Ocean Advocates at the Seattle Aquarium (grades 9–12)

ages.note: A drive is anyone's; the drop-off needs a lift.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, one drop-off.
details: The pantry accepts most unexpired food and clean supplies: open bags closed securely so they do not spill, anything out of its packaging labelled with the brand and the animal it is for, and prescription food if it is in date.
Drop-by hours on the pantry page are Thursdays, noon to 3pm, at the rescue at 20226 Ballinger Way NE in Shoreline; the giving page gives wider hours, so check the pantry page before you go.

The pantry depends on donations and cannot promise particular brands, so a drive that collects whatever people have is exactly what it runs on; email support@seattleareafelinerescue.org before bringing something large or specialised.
items.howTo: Tell neighbours and school what the pantry takes, collect it, and bring it to the Thursday drop-by hours.
items.location: Neighbourhood or school; drop off in Shoreline
items.summary: Seattle Area Feline Rescue runs a pet pantry for people who cannot afford to feed their cats. Collect food and bring it to the drop-by hours.
items.title: Food drive for the Stay SAFe Pet Pantry (Shoreline)

ages.note: The registered foster is an adult; the child helps at home.

details: Volunteers in the shelter must be at least 17, or 16 with an interview; for those under the required age, the rescue recommends discussing fostering with your family.
Foster scenarios include litters of kittens too young for adoption, bottle-baby kittens needing round-the-clock care, adult cats who need socialization, and adult cats with other needs.
Kittens come into the adoption center regularly for check-ups, normally 2–4 times a month; homes without regular transportation are welcome for adult cats in longer-term foster.
To start, read the Foster Handbook and fill out the online Foster Information Form.
items.howTo: Read the Foster Handbook on the foster page and submit the Foster Information Form.
items.summary: The rescue's shelter volunteers must be 16, and it points younger families to fostering.
items.title: Foster kittens or cats as a family (Seattle Area Feline Rescue)

ages.note: From 16; under 18 needs a parent's signature on the agreement.

details: The volunteer FAQ puts the minimum age at 16; anyone under 18 needs a parent or guardian's signature on the agreement.
Shifts are a regular weekly commitment of two to three hours.
Until then the rescue recommends fostering as a family (listed separately).
items.howTo: Apply through the volunteer page at 16, with a parent to sign the agreement.
items.summary: Cat care and adoption-center roles at the Shoreline rescue once she is old enough.
items.title: Seattle Area Feline Rescue volunteering (from 16)

ages.note: The parent is the registered volunteer; ask Education Services about her riding along.

details: Seattle Humane's volunteers are 18 and over, so the driver is the parent. The delivery role is the one the volunteer page describes as "a great opportunity to volunteer with a friend or family member" — a child can ride along and carry.
Deliveries go to clients of the Pet Food Bank, participating senior centres and food banks around the greater Seattle area.
Whether a child may come on a delivery shift is for Seattle Humane to say: ask Education Services, which handles youth and community service questions.
items.howTo: A parent applies for the delivery driver role on the volunteer page and emails EducationServices@seattlehumane.org to ask about bringing her.
items.location: Around Seattle, from the Bellevue shelter
items.summary: Drivers take pet food and supplies from Oogie's Ohana Pet Food Bank to clients, senior centres and food banks around Seattle. Seattle Humane calls it a great role to do with a family member.
items.title: Deliver pet food for Seattle Humane's pet food bank (the parent's role, with her along)

ages.note: A parent is the registered foster at 18+; the hour a day of playing and socialising is shared.

items.commitment: An hour a day, for as long as the cat needs.
details: The registered foster must be 18, and should expect to spend at least an hour a day socialising, playing with, feeding and caring for the animal.
A foster cat does not need the run of the house; a spare bedroom or even a spare bathroom is enough, and Seattle Humane recommends keeping foster and resident animals apart.
Seattle Humane can usually supply everything needed, though supplies come from donations and are limited.
It also runs a foster-to-adopt programme for cats and kittens with ringworm, training the family in its ringworm protocol.
items.howTo: Email foster@seattlehumane.org with a parent to apply, and ask what they most need fostered right now.
items.summary: About an hour a day of feeding, playing and socialising — most of which is the fun part.
items.title: Foster a cat or kitten for Seattle Humane

ages.note: Entering grades 9–12.

items.commitment: Individual shifts in December and January.
details: For students entering grades 9–12: assist with routine shelter tasks, meet other teens and earn community service hours that count toward the hours needed to graduate.
Tasks such as washing food and water bowls, cleaning crates, or packing pet food.
There is a $30 registration fee, which Seattle Humane says covers the staff time to train and supervise everyone.
Offered during winter months; students register for shifts in December and January.
items.howTo: Register on the High School Service Shifts page when winter registration opens; the fee is $30.
items.summary: Routine shelter tasks in winter that earn community service hours.
items.title: High School Service Shifts (grades 9–12)

ages.note: Ages 16–17.

items.commitment: Structured program; see the page for the schedule.
details: Designed for motivated 16–17-year-olds interested in animal welfare, community service, and career exploration in animal care.
Finishing it makes her eligible to apply for volunteer shifts at Seattle Humane, which is the door the younger programmes lead to.
items.howTo: Apply for HSTP through the Youth Programs page at 16.
items.summary: Structured, hands-on learning for older teens exploring animal-care careers.
items.title: High School Training Program (ages 16–17)

ages.note: No age limit stated on the page.

details: Old socks become catnip toys when stuffed with scrap paper, toilet paper tubes, or other crinkly items with catnip.
The project page lists more ways to make cat toys from recycled or reusable objects.
Community service hours are recorded on Seattle Humane's monthly Community Service Hours Log, one row per session with time in, time out and a signature (form linked on the organization).
items.howTo: Make the toys following the project page, then bring them to the shelter with any blankets.
items.location: At home; deliver to Seattle Humane
items.summary: Turn old socks and paper tubes into catnip toys for shelter cats.
items.title: Homemade cat toys from recycled objects

ages.note: Ages 13–17.

items.commitment: Two Saturdays a month during the school year.
details: For teens ages 13–17 to learn about Seattle Humane, explore animal welfare topics and prepare for future volunteer opportunities.
Members meet two Saturdays per month.
items.howTo: Sign up through the Youth Programs page when the school-year session opens.
items.summary: A school-year club for animal-loving teens at Seattle Humane.
items.title: Humane Teen Club (ages 13–17)
