ages.note: No age limit stated on the page.

items.commitment: One sitting per batch; drop off when you have a few.
details: All the cats in Seattle Humane's care receive a blanket or towel to make their cubby more comfortable; most of the time a cat's special blanket goes home with them when they are adopted.
Blankets around 18 × 20 inches are suggested for cats.
Written and video instructions for making no-sew blankets are on the project page.
Community service hours are recorded on Seattle Humane's monthly Community Service Hours Log, one row per session with time in, time out and a signature (form linked on the organization).
items.howTo: Follow the no-sew instructions on the project page, then bring the blankets to the shelter. Contact Education Services for drop-off details.
items.location: At home; deliver to Seattle Humane
items.summary: Make small fleece blankets for the cats waiting to be adopted.
items.title: No-sew cat blankets

ages.note: No age limit stated; collecting from neighbors and delivering needs an adult.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, then one delivery.
details: Donations of pet food, supplies and toys are always appreciated.

Food can be dropped at the lower parking lot at 13212 SE Eastgate Way without an appointment, or into the red Seattle Humane barrels at local Pet Pros shops; the in-kind donations page also carries an Amazon wish list.
Items are distributed through Oogie's Ohana Pet Food Bank at Seattle Humane, which helps provide 1 million meals each year to pets in the community.
Youth can help pets and earn school service hours by donating, fundraising or supporting the pet food bank.
Community service hours are recorded on Seattle Humane's monthly Community Service Hours Log, one row per session with time in, time out and a signature (form linked on the organization).
items.howTo: Pick a collection window, tell neighbors or the class what to bring, then deliver the donations to the shelter. Email Education Services for current needs.
items.location: Neighborhood or school; deliver to Seattle Humane
items.summary: Organize a pet food drive in the neighborhood or at school.
items.title: Pet food drive

ages.note: Not stated; an adult's role as described.

details: SPDR describes itself as volunteer-based, with placements handled by a team of volunteer Breed Representatives, and invites people to become one.
No minimum age or foster process is stated.
items.howTo: Ask about becoming a Breed Representative from the About page.
items.summary: A volunteer-run rescue that places purebred dogs through volunteer Breed Representatives, one breed each. No age on the page; it reads as an adult's role.
items.title: Seattle Purebred Dog Rescue breed representatives (age not stated)

ages.note: A drive is anyone's; the drop-off needs a lift.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, one drop-off.
details: The donation page names what helps most: dry and wet dog and cat food, leashes, collars and harnesses, dog and cat toys, flea treatment and dewormer, and poop bags.
Not accepted: opened food, controlled medications, or medicines more than a year past their date.

The page names Woodhaven Veterinary Hospital in Edmonds as the drop-off point, and an Amazon wish list for anything bought online; an older FAQ said any clinic location, so confirm the drop-off before going.
items.howTo: Collect from the most-needed list, keep food unopened, and take it to the drop-off the donation page names — or send people to the Amazon list.
items.location: Neighbourhood or school; drop off in Edmonds
items.summary: A Seattle nonprofit that brings vet care to the pets of people experiencing homelessness. Its most-needed list is ordinary pet-shop stuff a drive can collect.
items.title: Pet food and supplies for pets of people without homes (Seattle Veterinary Outreach)

ages.note: 12–13 with a parent, supervised throughout; 14–17 with a parent's approval.

items.commitment: Shifts, as arranged with the volunteer coordinator.
details: Volunteers are 18 and over; minors 14–17 may volunteer with parental approval, and minors 12–13 may volunteer with their parents and must be supervised at all times — all from the rescue's own volunteer page.
The rescue takes in horses that need rehabilitation and runs a Horses as Healers programme alongside the rescue work.
items.howTo: At 12, email volunteer@serenityequinerescue.com together and ask for the orientation and a shift the two of you can do.
items.summary: A horse rescue and rehabilitation farm south of Seattle whose volunteer page spells out the ages: 12 and 13 with their parents, 14 to 17 with a parent's approval.
items.title: Serenity Equine Rescue in Maple Valley (from 12, with a parent)

ages.note: From 16, with your own transport.

details: Teens over 16 with their own transportation can apply if they are available for regular shifts; for insurance and safety reasons there are no one-off tours or volunteer experiences for kids.
Cleaning shifts run on Sundays, Wednesdays or Fridays for two to four hours.
items.howTo: At 16, apply from the volunteer page.
items.summary: Cleaning shifts at a rabbit rescue in Carnation, for teens over 16 with their own transport; no tours or one-off experiences for children.
items.title: Special Bunny rabbit rescue in Carnation (from 16)

ages.note: Not stated.

details: The rescue is run primarily by volunteers; its homepage has an "interested in volunteering?" section with a volunteer application.
Older listings give a Puyallup address, newer ones Graham; no minimum age appears in either.
items.howTo: Fill in the volunteer application from the homepage and ask the minimum age.
items.summary: A volunteer-run rescue south of Puyallup, meeting mostly in Graham. The homepage links a volunteer application and states no age.
items.title: Sunny Sky's Animal Rescue in Graham (age not stated)

ages.note: A drive is anyone's; the drop-off needs a lift.

items.commitment: A few weeks of collecting, one drop-off.
details: Unopened, unexpired food and litter can be dropped at Entrance B (Adoptions), 10am to 5:30pm Tuesday to Sunday by the donate page — the pantry page says 5pm, so ring (253) 383-2733 if it matters.
A Chewy wish list ships food and litter straight to the shelter, which is the route without a drive to Tacoma.
The shelter says plainly that money goes further, because it buys at wholesale.
items.howTo: Collect dry food and litter, unopened, and take it to Entrance B in opening hours — or point people at the Chewy list.
items.location: Neighbourhood or school; drop off at 2608 Center Street, Tacoma
items.summary: Dry dog and cat food and cat litter are what the Tacoma shelter asks for first; they stock its pantry for families who cannot afford them.
items.title: Food and litter drive for Tacoma's Pet Food & Supply Pantry

ages.note: An adult registers; the distance rule, not the age, is what decides.

items.commitment: At least one foster a year.
details: Fosters are asked to live within Pierce County or within 25 miles of the shelter, so animals stay near it and its emergency vets; most of Seattle is outside that circle.
The shelter asks each foster home for at least one foster animal or litter a year, and runs a background check on every applicant.
No experience needed; food, toys, blankets and medical care are provided; the shelter named a pressing need for homes without other pets. Stays run from days to months.
items.howTo: If you live close enough to Tacoma, a parent applies from the foster page and goes through the background check.
items.location: At home, within 25 miles of Tacoma
items.summary: Fostering for the Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County, with food, supplies and vet care provided — but only for homes within 25 miles of the shelter.
items.title: Foster for the Tacoma shelter (Pierce County homes)

ages.note: From 16, no parent exception; dog roles from 18.

items.commitment: Six hours a month for six months.
details: Every volunteer must be at least 16, and the shelter says it cannot accommodate anyone under 16 even with a parent or guardian volunteering with them.
Dog walking and animal transport are 18 and over.
The commitment is at least six hours a month for at least six months, with a background check; students who need community service hours get them signed off only once the six months are done.
items.howTo: At 16, apply from the volunteer page and plan for the six-month commitment before counting on the hours.
items.summary: The big Tacoma shelter is 16 and over with no exception for a parent coming along; dogs are 18. Six hours a month for six months.
items.title: Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County shelter volunteering (from 16)

ages.note: Ages 8–13 per the youth page (6–10 per the event page); an adult comes along.

details: Youths 8–13 can register for one of NOAH's Kid's Day volunteer opportunities; regular volunteering starts at 14 (14–15 with a parent).
The Kid's Day page describes it as perfect for kids ages 6–10, all ages welcome with adult supervision, and each camper must be accompanied by an adult.
It costs $30 per child, runs 10am to 3pm, and takes 30 children per session, so it books up.

Kids 'adopt' a plush pet and walk it through intake, medical exams and adoption day, with stations like puppy paw painting, bottle-feeding baby animals, scent trails, agility demos and clicker training; snacks and water are provided, pack a lunch.
items.howTo: Watch the Kid's Volunteer Day page for the next date and register — $30 a child, thirty places, and an adult comes for the day.
items.location: The NOAH Center, 31300 Brandstrom Rd, Stanwood
items.summary: A hands-on day at the Stanwood shelter: kids follow a plush pet through the shelter journey and meet the real dogs and cats.
items.title: Kid's Volunteer Day at The NOAH Center

ages.note: From 18.

details: The volunteer page sets the minimum at 18. Questions go to waifvc@waifanimals.org.
WAIF runs educational workshops for school-age children, which are something to attend rather than a role.
items.howTo: At 18, email the volunteer coordinator from the volunteer page.
items.summary: Whidbey's shelter takes volunteers from 18 and does not offer court-ordered placements; its school-age programmes are presentations, not volunteering.
items.title: WAIF on Whidbey Island (from 18)

ages.note: 16 alone, or 15 with a parent volunteering alongside.

items.commitment: One four-hour shift a week, the same day and time.
details: Youth volunteers must be 16, or 15 with a parent alongside.
It is a standing commitment: one four-hour shift a week, the same day and time every week, after an orientation and the mandatory trainings.

The work includes helping in the nursery feeding baby animals, preparing diets, cleaning the hospital wards, cages and enclosures, and the sweeping, mopping, dishes and laundry that a hospital runs on.
Training is given for every role and no experience is needed; volunteers also help make events work.
Orphaned wild songbirds and opossums are among the animals named as needing feeding.
items.howTo: At 15, apply together through the wildlife volunteer page and pick the weekly slot you can both keep — the ferry trip is part of the day.
items.summary: Feeding orphaned songbirds and baby opossums at a wildlife hospital — when she is fifteen.
items.title: West Sound Wildlife Shelter (from 15 with a parent)

ages.note: Entering grades 10–12.

items.commitment: Twenty hours of summer shifts, plus orientation and seven cohort meetings.
details: The Teen Ambassador programme is open to teens entering grades 10–12; it lets them explore different departments within the zoo, from animal care to horticulture, and talk to visitors at exhibits and camps.
It is a summer: an orientation day at the zoo in late June, at least seven cohort meetings, and twenty hours of shifts between the end of June and early September.
Applying is a spring job — the zoo invites the people it selects to interview in mid-April, so the application closes before that.
items.howTo: Apply in the spring, before the mid-April interviews, for the summer that follows — the page says when the window opens.
items.summary: Teens explore zoo departments from animal care to horticulture and help teach at exhibits and camps.
items.title: Woodland Park Zoo Teen Ambassadors (grades 10–12)

ages.note: No age stated; no account needed to start.

details: ZSL's Instant Wild brings images and videos from camera traps around the world; identifying the species you spot helps track threatened wildlife and their ecosystems.
No qualifications or special expertise are needed; lots of help is provided to make the right identification.
You can start online at instantwild.zsl.org without creating an account, or use the free iOS or Android app; an account adds badges for milestones.
items.howTo: Open instantwild.zsl.org or the app and start tagging; log the time as an entry.
items.summary: Photos arrive from cameras around the world as animals walk past; you say what you see.
items.title: Tag wildlife in live camera-trap photos (Instant Wild)

ages.note: No age limit; under 16 a parent approves the account.

items.commitment: Any time, ten minutes or an hour.
details: Hundreds of camera traps in Serengeti National Park, Tanzania, produce millions of images; volunteers identify the species, count individuals, classify behaviour and note whether young are present.
There is no age limit for Zooniverse projects, but children under 16 need a parent or guardian to sign off on their account registration.

The project is described as ideally suited to primary and elementary school children, combining ecology, geography and literacy; Zooniverse also publishes guidance on fulfilling service-hour requirements.
items.howTo: Create her Zooniverse account with a parent's approval, open Snapshot Serengeti, and classify together; log the time as an entry.
items.summary: Real research from home: name the animals in camera-trap photos from Serengeti National Park.
items.title: Classify Serengeti camera-trap animals (Zooniverse)

ages.note: Seek needs no account at any age. An iNaturalist account requires 13+, or a parent's permission and help setting it up under 13; eBird runs on a parent's Cornell Lab account.

details: Seek by iNaturalist identifies plants and animals from the camera, needs no login and is made for children; observations can be posted on to iNaturalist itself.
iNaturalist's own records feed research datasets; eBird, run by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, does the same for bird checklists and needs a free Cornell Lab account.
Observations are made outdoors and uploaded from a phone or computer.
items.howTo: Start with the Seek app, which needs no sign-up; to have the sightings count as data, post them on to iNaturalist from a parent-supervised account, or record bird checklists in eBird on a parent's Cornell Lab account. Log the time as an entry.
items.summary: Turn walks in the park into wildlife records scientists use.
items.title: Log the birds and animals you see (Seek and eBird)
